You have to recharge them during the day. For active people that means you have to carry the recharge gadgets with you and awkward situations during the day etc. When a disaster arrives, I will be deaf within a few days without a recharging option.Batteries i can buy in multitude and take with me wherever I go. When i look at the new models from several brands I see not a single model with battery supply (e.g. ReSound Enzo Q IA, Phonak Audéo Sphere). Are there more of you that are worried about this? can we do something about this?

Factory side here, we build OTC aids in China for other brands. Nobody in 173 posts has been on the manufacturing end of this, so rather than re-argue the preference I'd rather answer the two things that got left open.

user_119 is right in #22 and that's worth saying plainly. The top DSP platform being rechargeable only is a product decision, not a physics limit. We do the same thing. When you segment a lineup, the feature that costs nothing to withhold is the one that ships on the newer housing, and the newer housing is sealed. So people who want the best processing get moved to rechargeable whether or not they ever wanted to leave batteries. Calling that a customer preference is doing a lot of work.

Where the mechanism usually gets told wrong is the current argument. It isn't average draw. A 312 runs a modern DSP perfectly well. What it struggles with is the peak while the LE Audio radio is transmitting, because zinc air has high internal impedance and the voltage sags under bursts. You can engineer around that with a 675 and more bulk capacitance.

Which is david.hendon's question in #77, whether anyone actually knows if it could be made to work. It could. A 675 aid with a de rated streaming profile is buildable today. It doesn't get built because the volume isn't there to pay for a separate housing tool, and housing tooling is where the money goes.

The part I should hand over rather than wait to be asked about is the battery door. It's the most expensive piece of the shell. A hinge, two contacts and a hole through the case. It's the single biggest leak path for an IP rating and it's a large share of mechanical warranty returns. Delete it and the factory gains a sealing spec, loses a failure mode and drops an assembly step. So the honest answer to the thread title is both, and the factory half of that is real and it isn't small.

And the cost of it lands on the buyer in a way that mostly gets left out here. A sealed cell has an end date. Around year four or five it wants replacing as a paid service, and on older platforms that service quietly stops being offered, at which point something repairable has become something replaceable. user_119 has the direction of the incentive right even where the mechanism was off.

Happy to be checked on any of it.
